titulo: Three biases that drive a purchase
lead: Nobody decides with a spreadsheet alone. Three mental shortcuts show up in almost every purchase: losing hurts more than gaining, nobody wants to be the first, and what has already been invested weighs heavily. You will recognize them, use them only with true facts, and know exactly where the line is. This is where trust lives.
objetivo: use loss aversion, social proof and sunk effort only with true facts, and apply the test that separates influence from manipulation.

aprende.t: What a decision bias is, and what a reframe is
Loss aversion, social proof and sunk effort
Honest social proof when you still have few clients
The test that separates influence from manipulation

hero_alt: Two adults in a bright meeting room comparing two sheets of paper side by side, looking thoughtful.

secoes.sub: The decision is felt first and rationalized later. Click each shortcut.

nos.detalhe: "You'll save money" persuades less than "you're losing money," even with the same number. Use the numbers they gave you in the diagnosis and their own unit of time: per week hurts more than per year.

nos.titulo: Nobody wants to be the first
nos.detalhe: People want to know that someone like them, with a similar problem, has already walked this path. Industry and company size are enough; the client's name isn't needed.
Six months of trying to solve it internally weigh heavily at the table. Acknowledge the effort and ask the right question: from here on, what is the best path?
The person will justify the decision with numbers later, even to their business partner. But the movement started with one of these three shortcuts.

secoes.legenda: To reframe is to state the same fact from another angle. "Saves ten hours a week" and "loses ten hours a week" describe the same reality.
secoes.dica: Working with biases is not deceiving: it's presenting the true information in a way the person can process.

secoes.sub: How to use each one, and how each one backfires.

texto: Gain: "your proposal goes out in three hours instead of three days," true and easy to postpone. Loss: "every week your proposal takes three days is one more client who closes with whoever replied first."
Never invent a false deadline or artificial scarcity.
A project done for free, with the result recorded, is legitimate proof, as long as you say that's how it was. An observed pattern counts too.
Anonymize it: "a dental clinic with four chairs". Inflating results or inventing a client works until the second question.
Honest use: "you've already put about six months into this. How much more does it make sense to invest before bringing in someone who has done it before?".
Backfires: "you wasted six months," said with the person who led the attempt in the room. Someone who just bought a tool will defend it: propose adding to it, not replacing it.

passos.titulo: Spread them out, don't stack them
texto: After the number, name the loss. When they hesitate, bring in a similar case. Before the close, acknowledge the effort.
All three in a row sound like a salesperson's argument. Spread out, they look like what they are: honest observations at the right moment.

secoes.titulo: The line between influence and manipulation
secoes.sub: The test: if the client knew exactly what you are doing, would they still be comfortable?

texto: Use the numbers they gave you themselves. Cite a real case, anonymized.
Say what the solution does not do. This is what Professional 2030 calls trust: saying what you know and what you don't know how to do.

passos.sub: the same mechanism, a false fact
texto: Made-up deadlines and scarcity. Inflated numbers or a fictional client.

passos.titulo: Why the line is in your interest
texto: A client convinced by pressure cancels, pays late and complains at delivery. A client convinced by a true argument refers others, and referrals arrive at the bottom of the pipeline.
And someone who sells by pushing ends up hating selling, and goes back to square one of lesson 1.

secoes.sub: Reframing is writing work, not improvisation.

blocos.conteudo:
You are my editor of sales arguments. I will give you FACTS. You may only use those facts.
WHAT I SELL: <one sentence: AI diagnostic, audit, mentorship or training>
TYPICAL CLIENT: <sector and size>
FACTS I HAVE (do not invent any others):
- <e.g.: in 3 projects, the quote response time dropped from 2 days to 2 hours>
- <e.g.: I have never served this specific sector>
- <e.g.: my pilot takes 3 weeks>
Write, in US English and in a conversational tone:
1. THREE "cost of staying as is" sentences, using the client's own numbers
   as variables marked like this: <number they said>.
2. THREE HONEST social proof sentences based on the facts above, anonymized
   (sector and size, never a name). If a fact cannot support social proof, say so.
3. TWO sentences that acknowledge the effort the company has already made, without sounding condescending.
4. A list of what I CANNOT claim with the facts I have.
Hard rule: no made-up urgency, no number that I did not give you.

secoes.sub: Your bank of sentences, built only from your own facts.

exercicios.texto: List the facts you really have (projects, results, what you have never done) and run the prompt. Save the result in a file of your own.
exercicios.pronto: the file has sentences for all three biases and item 4 (what you cannot claim) is filled in; if it came back empty, you redid it.

exercicios.texto: Reread the sentences you usually use in a sales conversation. Apply the test to each one: would the client be comfortable knowing what you are doing?
exercicios.pronto: you marked each sentence as influence or manipulation and rewrote or cut the ones that did not pass.

secoes.sub: 4 questions. The explanation appears after your attempt.

perguntas.p: What is the test that separates influence from manipulation?
opcoes: If the client closed, it was influence; if they refused, it was manipulation
If the client knew exactly what you are doing, would they still be comfortable
If the technique is well known, it can be used without restriction
perguntas.explica: Both sides use the same mental mechanism. What changes is whether the fact behind it is true.

perguntas.p: You still have few clients. What is a legitimate social proof?
opcoes: Citing a big company as if it were a client
A project done for free, with the result recorded, saying that's how it was
perguntas.explica: Fragile proof told honestly is worth more than strong proof made up, which falls apart at the second question.

perguntas.p: The manager who led six months of internal attempts is in the room. How do you use sunk effort?
opcoes: "You've already put in a lot of time. The question now is what the shortest path is from here."
perguntas.explica: Acknowledging the effort guides the next decision; dismissing it makes you the adversary of the people in the room.

perguntas.p: Why spread the three phrases across the conversation?
opcoes: Because together they sound like a salesperson's pitch and trigger distrust
You don't need to spread them out
perguntas.explica: Spread out, each one shows up at the right hook as an honest observation. Stacked together, they become a speech.

itens.texto: The same fact, said as a loss, moves people more, using the client's own numbers.

itens.t: Nobody wants to be the first
itens.texto: Anonymized social proof can be built even with few clients.

itens.t: The line is the truth of the fact
